column2: Just then a party arrived, led by Changgen, followed by Yu Wucheng, then You Laowu and his fellow men of the brotherhood, with Yang Fengmao and Zhu bringing up the rear. The room was packed. Miaozhen and her maids hurried to attend them, adding to the confusion. Drawing Hu away from Gu and Liu, You whispered, “Little Uncle, I have something important to discuss. Where can we find somewhere quiet?” Hu asked Miaozhen, who answered at once, “Miaozhu's room is empty.” “Of course! That reminds me. What's happened to her?” Miaozhen gave him an odd glance. Her voice was half reproachful, half teasing. “I should be asking what's happened to you, Master Hu.” Once begun, that conversation would never end. Concerned though he was, Hu had no time to inquire. “We'll discuss it later,” he said, and turned away. He took You to Miaozhu's former room and felt the difference as soon as he entered. The bedding and pillows had been removed from the great brass bed where Gu had slept, leaving only its rattan base. The cosmetics had vanished from the dressing table; even the mirror was covered with cloth. Everything spoke of the desolation of an empty room whose occupant had gone, who knew where. Unconsciously, Hu sighed. You had spent the day discussing important business and knew nothing of this. “Why are you sighing, Little Uncle?” Hu was moved by all Miaozhu had undergone in a single day, from attempting to end her life to firmly leaving the courtesan's world. But these were private feelings. Why speak of them now? He answered only, “How did your talks with Changgen go?”

“That was a small matter. He's formidable, of course, but among our own people he mustn't speak ‘French’.” “What?” Hu interrupted. “What language?” You laughed. “It's a saying recently current in the settlement. Some people understand English, but when a man speaks French, you only hear his tongue rolling and have no idea what he's saying. So when someone talks only to suit himself and neither side can ever agree, we call it speaking French.” “A good expression. If Changgen wasn't speaking French, what was he speaking?” “Plain truth. Everyone has a heart. After the way you've treated him, he can't behave like a fool. He also said, ‘Food won't make you poor, nor will clothes; a lack of judgement will keep you poor all your life.’ That's sound enough. We all look to you now.” His tone became solemn. “Little Uncle, from now on the Grain Transport Brotherhood north and south of the Yangtze will depend on you.” “You honour me too much!” Hu was astonished. “How does that follow?” “We've discussed it.” You spoke slowly. “We all want you as our strategist, to give us our direction. Don't interrupt. Let me finish.” He described a plan for the brotherhood's survival. Since the rising of Hong and Yang had blocked the waterways and grain tribute had been diverted to sea transport, its members had struggled to make a living. War raged everywhere, local militias were forming for self-defence, and the court could scarcely cope with military affairs, much less attend to the brotherhood's livelihood. Its leaders understood these difficulties. Whenever junior members caused trouble, they urged them patiently to endure the hard times together. But every household had mouths to feed, old people and children alike. Kind advice alone could not fill empty stomachs. You, Yu, Changgen and other leaders had therefore reached the same conclusion: they must find a livelihood for themselves. “Everyone admires your intelligence as the finest in the world, Little Uncle. You must not only find us a path, but lead us along it.”

Hu drew a breath, already feeling the crushing weight on his shoulders. Yet he could not refuse. He could only find a way. Naturally, You and his companions had not merely adopted a grand aim and thrust the whole burden on him. They had discussed several possible courses, though most were inspired by Hu's own ideas. “First, we have boats and men. If we can't carry tribute grain, we can carry other goods, even passengers. There are so many refugees now that finding a berth can be difficult. Wouldn't that be good business?” “Certainly. The difficulty is whether the authorities will permit it. I'll try to find a way.” “Exactly!” You was delighted. “That's why we want you to lead us. We need your help to clear those obstacles.” “I can't promise they can be cleared. What other businesses did you discuss?” “Exports of silk and tea seem certain to recover. We thought of pooling capital and asking you to trade for us.” “That is possible. But first, would the profits belong to individuals or to the whole body?” You was taken aback. “True. I hadn't considered that. We're asking you to find a livelihood for our brothers. If the profits are shared by everyone, naturally there's no objection. Otherwise that business must wait.” “That's my view too.” Hu hesitated, then asked, “Brother Five, are your own intentions public or...” “You know my situation. There's no distinction between public and private. When there's money, I first set aside the Old Master's expenses. The rest is for everyone. Those who reach farther take more; those who move slowly take less.” “That won't do. You must establish rules. Never mind being the leader of a branch—even in my own business I must treat the employees fairly if I want them sincerely to accept things.” You nodded earnestly. “You're right.” “Ask Old Gu to advise you on that. We needn't discuss it now. We should certainly trade in silk and tea, but there must be other businesses that can provide food for everyone. When I have some leisure, I'll think them through for you.”

“Good. I wanted to explain first. The others will have more to say at dinner.” That night's banquet was given expressly by the brotherhood as a whole. It was no trap, yet the meal was hard to endure. The more they praised Hu, the heavier his responsibility felt. As he answered modestly, he reflected that sometimes a man moving in their world had to put on a bold front, promising everything even beyond his ability. Sometimes he had to charge ahead, whether he could accomplish a thing or not. But sometimes neither pretence nor a headlong charge would do: honesty must come first, steadiness second. This was such an occasion. Even if he carried off the bluff or forced his way through, he might gain little credit. If he failed, he would ruin important affairs for others and earn only blame for his efforts. That would be folly. When their speeches ended, he spoke calmly. “Brother You has explained your wishes. You honour me so greatly that I cannot refuse. But there are two things I must make clear first.” First, his own business and the many other affairs he had undertaken had reached a point where further delay was impossible. He could not immediately devote himself to the brotherhood. Second, he sighed, “Doing the work is easier than dealing with people.” He could not hope to satisfy everyone and asked for their understanding. They all readily accepted the first point. The second, however tactfully expressed, made several uneasy. Yu in particular laboured to assure him that nobody harboured any prejudice and that he must not suspect them. Hu was wary of the familiar saying, “Hemp has many fibres; worldly men have many suspicions.” He had meant to say more on the subject, but now held his tongue. By the time the drinking ended, the stars had wheeled far across the sky. Everyone except Changgen returned to the Zhu house to sleep.

With the Tongli business finished and much still awaiting him in Songjiang and Shanghai, You decided to leave early next morning. He came especially to say goodbye to Hu, but once they began talking there was no end to it. Hu repeatedly urged him to go, yet he was reluctant to leave. There would be other chances to say all this; they had simply met again after a long separation and hated to part so soon. They talked until dawn. You decided to board at once and sleep on the way to Songjiang. Since his friends were travelling with him, courtesy obliged Hu to see them off. After their handclasps by the river, Hu was exhausted and ready to return to Zhu's and bury himself in bed. Gu, beside him, caught his arm. “Look!” A small sedan chair swept past. Through its two glass windows Hu could see a woman, but not her face. “Who is it?” “Who else?” Gu smiled. “What other woman in Tongli concerns you?” He plainly meant Miaozhu. Hu felt unfairly cornered by the insistence that he cared for her. Before he could find an answer to accompany his rueful smile, the chair turned into a lane. “Where did she move to yesterday?” he blurted out. “Perhaps this very lane. Let's see.” Gu drew him to its entrance. Sure enough, the chair had stopped. Since they were there, Hu thought he might as well see for himself, and needed no further urging. The first thing he saw was a new sheet of scarlet paper bearing two enormous, shining black characters: “Hu Residence”. “Old Gu!” he asked in alarm. “Is Miaozhu's surname Hu too?” “I don't know.” “This is strange! Such high-handed compulsion—I've never seen the like. I must ask Miaozhen when we get back.”

“Why go to that trouble? Miaozhu is here. Why not ask her?” Before Hu could stop him, Gu lifted the brass ring and knocked twice. The black-lacquered doors opened. The maid with hanging hair was A’jin, Miaozhu's attendant. Her round face looked like one of Wuxi's plump clay dolls, and she greeted them with a smile. “Master Hu! Have you eyes that see a thousand li and ears that hear on the wind? You've found us so early.” Hu had no wish to joke. “Where is Second Miss?” “Just back.” Before she finished, Miaozhu lifted the curtain and appeared. In a plain cloth jacket and skirt, without cosmetics, she already looked like a woman of a respectable household. “Mr Gu, please come in.” She smiled and cast Hu a glance in greeting, as though everything between them went without saying. She was taking the position of mistress of the Hu household. There was no need to ask her surname now. The problem was how to persuade her to remove that notice. Keeping his expression unchanged, Hu said, “A good house. Clever of you to find it. You decide to move, and at once there's a suitable place. What a coincidence.” “Yes, very fortunate! Let me show you.” She led them from front to back, then seated them in the reception room. The furniture seemed to have come with the house; trunks and other belongings still stood unpacked in the corners. “It's all in disorder today, with nowhere to sit. Next time will be better, Mr Gu. The silk trade must bring you to Tongli. If you need somewhere to stay, come here. Treat it as your own home.” Gu thanked her. “Whenever I come to Tongli, I'll certainly visit.”

There was no more talk of religious devotion! Hu was inwardly amused. He wanted to tease her but feared angering her and restrained himself. Still, he could not quite suppress the smile of a man who had caught someone out. “What are you laughing at?” she asked. “That I act without thinking ahead?” Those words invited reflection, but Hu did not pursue them. “Is this house rented, held under a redeemable transfer, or bought?” “Rented.” “Would the landlord sell?” “We could discuss it.” “You seem very fond of it.” He paused. “To save trouble, I might as well buy it for you.” “As you wish.” “Then first take down the ‘Hu Residence’ notice.” “No.” Her refusal was firm. “My surname is Hu. Why shouldn't I put it up?” “Weren't you going to turn the place into a private nunnery?” “Exactly. Then I'll replace it with ‘Hu Family Nunnery’.” “As you please. There are plenty of people called Hu. Call yourself whatever you like.” Again his words held her at a distance. She felt he was being too cold, and her face darkened.

Exhausted and irritable, Hu thought her obstinate and unreasonable. He almost wanted to quarrel and let the quarrel end everything. Before he could speak, Gu saw the danger and intervened. “Ah!” He stared at Miaozhu in apparent horror, like a man suddenly remembering some gravely neglected matter. Both fell for the distraction. “What's wrong?” Hu asked first. Gu relaxed, shaking his head. “Nothing. I remember now. It's all right.” Miaozhu patted her chest. “You really do frighten people!” Hu was naturally much more concerned about Gu than she was. “What did you remember? What's all right?” There was nothing to explain, so Gu improvised. “A very amusing story came to mind.” Hu did not know whether to laugh or cry. Miaozhu found it absurd: was Mr Gu subject to some disorder? Seeing Hu's vexed, helpless expression, she burst out laughing. At least one side was now soothed. Gu could see that a little tenderness from her would turn the hardest steel soft. He gave her a glance, then pointed to Hu. “He talked with Master You all night, saw him aboard, and then came to see you. He's truly exhausted. Let him have a proper sleep.” He rose to leave, watching Hu closely. When Hu tried to rise too, Gu turned and firmly pressed him back into his chair. “Zhu's house is full of people coming and going, far too noisy. You've worn yourself out these past few days. Now that several important affairs are taking shape, rest properly and regain your strength. Tomorrow we'll go together to Suzhou and then Shanghai.” “Mr Gu means well,” Miaozhu said calmly. “One should know good advice from bad and listen to the good.” Hu could scarcely keep his eyes open. Under their persuasion, his last resistance gave way like water running downhill. He was too weary even to speak. But as Gu reached the door, he remembered something essential. “Wait, Old Gu. Zhou may return from Suzhou today. If there's any news, send someone to tell me at once.” “I understand. Rest here without worry.”

Once Gu had gone, Miaozhu wrung out a hot towel herself and handed it to Hu. “Are you hungry?” “Not hungry. I feel rather empty inside.” “It's your body that's weak. I've been simmering lotus-seed porridge. Have a bowl, then go to bed.” She left, and soon A’jin brought a bowl on a Fujian lacquer tray: lotus-seed porridge with osmanthus and rock sugar. Hu liked sweet things. It was delicate, rich, sweet and soft, and he wanted more when it was gone. As though anticipating his thought, Miaozhu immediately brought a second bowl. “I didn't expect you, so I made little. This is the last bowl. I'll put more on, ready when you wake. What else would you like? I can begin preparing it early.” Her tenderness swept away his defences. Once A’jin was out of earshot, he smiled. “Nothing else. Only you.” He reached to draw her towards him, but she twisted away lightly. “A gentleman uses words; a small-minded man uses his hands,” she teased. Hu laughed, stretched and rose. Miaozhu led him to a spacious bedroom, not yet fully arranged, but with curtains hung and clean bedding ready. He sank onto the bed and would not move. “Get up a moment so I can make it properly.” “It's good enough.” His eyes were already closing. “I don't want to move.” Helplessly, she called A’jin. Together they removed his boots and loosened his clothes, turning him this way and that with considerable effort. His head had barely reached the pillow before he was snoring.

He slept until afternoon. The first thing he heard was a soft, languid tune hummed through the nose. Turning towards the room, he looked through the white mesh curtains and saw Miaozhu combing her hair by the window. It reached her waist, too long for a single stroke; she had to lift a smooth white arm and take the ends in her other hand. The sight stirred him. He coughed, and when she lifted the curtain to look, he quickly pulled her towards him. Taken by surprise, she protested, “Always so rough!” When he released her, she stepped back and said seriously, “This is a different place now.” Hu paused, then understood. She was a respectable woman now, no longer keeping a courtesan's house with her sister. Overnight, her status had changed. But was it not absurd to say this to a man lying in her bed? Without thinking, he asked, “Then what am I, sleeping here?” “Ask yourself. Until you explain, I can only treat you as a guest.” “A guest!” He could not help laughing. “A guest sleeping in the hostess's bed!” She too suppressed a smile, then grew stern again. “Just this once. Next time, I'm afraid...” “What? You'll turn me out?” Unable to answer, she called A’jin for washing water. Though she attended him, she kept her distance, as if afraid he would lay hands on her. Her manner, as though facing a snake, offended Hu. He could not resist a taunt. “You really look the respectable woman now! Planning a chastity arch?” The words were harsh. Miaozhu changed colour, restrained her anger and answered with a cold smile. “Say what you like. I've made up my mind: until you show me your true heart, I won't leave you in peace. Wait. Trouble will come to your door.” It sounded like coercion, or a threat, but more than either like a lover's petulance. Hu laughed. “Tell me how you'll trouble me.” “I won't tell you. A heartless man deserves no pity. Just wait. One day you'll beg for mercy.”

Knowing that love lay beneath the anger, Hu still could not help laughing. “What irreconcilable feud is there between us, that you hate me so?” Miaozhu had spoken impulsively. The release had pleased her, but now regret followed. His question made her reconsider the few days behind them. A man of his position visiting pleasure houses was nothing unusual. If every man who liked her had to bring wealth and marry her, where would that lead? Taking a concubine was less momentous than marrying a wife, but it was no small matter. Naturally, he had difficulties. Her whole heart was fixed on him, making his feelings seem shallow by comparison. Yet as a guest he had observed every proper obligation. She could only blame her own one-sided longing and stubborn pursuit of it. Her distress had no outlet. Self-pity, self-reproach and shame brought tears she could not stop. Sitting at the dressing table, facing away, she let them soak the front of her clothes without even wiping her eyes. Hu, seated behind her on the bed, could not see her face. Her motionless silence seemed strange. Only when he came round did he understand. “Why? What's happened? Why such grief?” After crying, she felt clearer and less entangled in her emotions. “I've thought it through. Everyone has their own circumstances. Forcing ourselves together is pointless. I certainly won't go back, but I won't cling to you any longer either.” She wiped her eyes, blew her nose and left the room. Hu should have felt relieved, yet instead he felt empty. He sat in her chair, bewildered. Unable to remain still, he wandered to the window and happened to see her holding a red sheet with writing on it. The meaning was plain: she had taken down the ‘Hu Residence’ notice. He felt a strange sense of loss. When she returned empty-handed and said nothing, he could hardly ask first. Awkwardly, he said, “Why hasn't Old Gu come? What time is it?”

“Almost three.” Her manner had changed, acquiring the formality of a hostess entertaining a guest. “Would you like a meal or some refreshments first?” “I'll combine lunch and dinner. I'm not hungry. Which restaurant is good? Order a banquet for this evening. I'll borrow your house to entertain.” She seemed hesitant, but nodded. “Whom are you inviting?” “Our usual friends. Zhu is the guest of honour. We've imposed on him for days. I ought to show my appreciation.” “Ordering food is simple enough. But if you've just decided, you must tell your guests quickly.” “Yes. I'll go myself.” She helped him into his long gown and saw him out. Only after the doors closed did he turn to look. The scarlet notice had indeed gone, though its four dark-red corners still clung to the wood, like the remnants of a festive announcement after the celebration had ended. He felt the melancholy of a finished song and departed company. After standing there a long while, he turned away. At the mouth of the lane was a stationer's. He bought a sheet of tiger-patterned paper and, looking at the large inkstone on the counter, asked, “Who here has a good hand? Would someone write two characters for me?” The apprentice pointed to a white-bearded old man smoking a water pipe beside the accounts desk. “Our old proprietor's writing is splendid.” The old man rose with his pipe and a welcoming smile. Once told what Hu wanted, he took the brush and wrote in a single sweep. Despite his years, his wrist was strong. In the dignified manner of Wei inscriptions, the characters ‘Hu Residence’ looked elegant and imposing. The sheet was trimmed. Keeping the errand with the same shop, Hu asked the apprentice to bring paste, led him to Miaozhu's house and had the notice quietly fixed to the doorpost. Then he hired a small chair and went to Zhu's.

He met Zhou as soon as he entered. Zhou had arrived at noon, but Gu, mindful of Hu's exhaustion, had deliberately kept him from disturbing his sleep. Naturally, they discussed the important business first. He Guiqing had been pleased by the letter and had acted energetically, going at once to the governor-general's office. The military affairs office had appointed an expectant assistant prefect named Xi as commissioner in sole charge of the matter. Assistant Prefect Xi would come to Tongli within a day or two to meet Changgen. “I know Xi very well,” Yu put in. “He's exceptionally capable and generous-minded. A good friend.” Hu was delighted and bowed deeply. “Elder Brother, I must trouble you. I was worrying that I couldn't get away. Now I can leave it all to you. I'll keep Old Zhou here to follow your instructions.” “It's everyone's business. Why speak of troubling me?” Yu readily agreed. “I know these other affairs have delayed much of your proper work. Leave this to me. When do you go?” “Tomorrow, without fail.” Hu took the opportunity to invite them. “I've imposed on Zhu for several days and have no way to show my thanks. I've borrowed a place to entertain you tonight. Old Gu knows where. He'll bring you.” “What sort of place? Is it convenient? I dislike entertaining among strangers.” “Entirely convenient,” Gu answered for him. “You won't feel constrained.” The guests were invited, but Hu remained concerned about Miaozhu. With only A’jin to help, might the two women find the arrangements too much? He took Zhou back to ‘Hu Residence’ to assist.

His anxiety proved unnecessary. Miaozhu had hired half a ‘tea-chest’ service to provide tea, warm the wine and wait at table. The restaurant had sent three men as well: a cook, an assistant and a man for odd jobs and serving. With so many attending to one table, the hostess had nothing to do. She stood at ease in the corridor, cracking melon seeds and looking about. “Old Zhou, you've come at just the right time. Would you borrow some gaming sets for me?” These were indispensable to the entertainment. Zhou fetched mahjong tiles, pai gow tiles and a dice-shaking bowl from Zhu's. The arrangements were barely complete when the whole party arrived. Gu led the way. At once he asked Miaozhu, “Why replace a notice that had only just been put up?” She stared. “What notice?” “Those two characters, of course. Surely you know?” She truly did not. Argument was useless, so she ran outside. There stood ‘Hu Residence’ on tiger-patterned paper. The ink was already dry; it had not just been pasted up. Who had done it? Could it be Hu? If so, when? Perhaps Gu, always eager to help, had persuaded Hu to relent and offer this reassurance. But no: Gu knew nothing of the quarrel or her removal of the old sign. Why would he have acted? Hu himself must have changed his mind. At last she had moved him to surrender and bow before her charms. She was triumphant, and happier and more touched still. Back inside, Hu looked at her and smiled, confirming that he had done it. But when? Even in such a small matter, he moved mysteriously. What a formidable man! She must admire him—and be careful. She returned a smile of perfect understanding. Gu saw it and grew more curious, but he had guests to help entertain and could not investigate.

“It's early for dinner,” Liu said, already eagerly gathering players. “What shall we play? Let Elder Yu decide.” “We're all friends. We mustn't take it seriously. Today Miaozhu has left her old life, and we ought to make a gesture. Let everyone judge my proposal: rotating banks at pai gow, with no winnings pocketed. Everything goes towards buying her something.” Hu hastily declined. “There's no such custom!” Everyone else approved, but he continued to refuse. Bluntly, Yu asked, “Old Hu, are you afraid we'll make you lose face?” Hu disliked the words, but had to show alarm. “Elder Brother, how can you say that? I can only be silent now.” “Exactly!” Yu laughed. “Nothing else would stop your objections. I'm a little older, so I'll take the first bank.” It was an unusual game. Everyone wanted to lose a little for Miaozhu's benefit, and the result was almost a balance. When Yu, Liu, Gu and Yang had each banked, only two hundred and fifty taels remained in profit. “Not enough. Again!” Yu gathered the tiles and shuffled. “The small game this time. Bet freely.” The players could hardly make small wagers now. There were sixteen hundred taels on the table. Yu threw the dice and dealt, glanced at his tiles, then kept them face down without a word. The three gates revealed respectable hands. He turned his over lightly: a pair, beating them all. “Enough! I thank you for Miaozhu.” He pushed the tiles away, gathered the banknotes in the centre and rose smiling. In all Liu's years of gambling, he had never seen a set of pai gow end after a single deal. Losing was secondary; his appetite had been roused and left unsatisfied. But he could only stop. Gu felt differently. “Elder Yu acts as briskly as he speaks. That's the spirit I admire.”

Already pleased with himself, Yu grew more excited at the praise. Without thinking, he announced, “Let's do another fine, decisive thing today. Once I say it, everyone will agree. But Old Hu mustn't speak.” “Why not?” Hu protested with a smile. “You might spoil the occasion.” Gu had already guessed his intention. Afraid that Yu would speak and Hu refuse, turning a happy plan into a deadlock, he hurried to intervene. “Elder Yu, come here a moment.” Drawing him aside, he found he was right. Yu meant to unite Hu and Miaozhu at once. The banquet was ready to serve as their wedding feast; the guests and gifts were there too. With the marriage settled, Hu could return to Suzhou tomorrow and attend to business. “Little Uncle will certainly appreciate your kindness. But every household has its own difficult scripture. We don't yet know his troubles. Your word carries great weight. Once you've spoken, he cannot refuse. Yet you wouldn't want him to harbour private misgivings. Friends should leave one another no cause for regret. Don't you agree?” Yu did not understand the formal phrase, but grasped the meaning readily. On reflection, he had been rash. Once spoken, the words could not be recalled; if matters went wrong, his own dignity would suffer. He felt a new respect for Gu. “Quite right. You've thought it through. What should we do?” Gu knew Yu's love of excitement, and his spoilt young master's belief that a well-meant offer must never be refused. Reflecting that Hu had softened towards Miaozhu and a happy outcome seemed possible, he agreed to inquire privately.

Hu's answer astonished him. “I've already sent Zhou to fetch Miaozhen. As soon as Elder Yu spoke, I understood. Since things have reached this point, you two can discuss it with her when she comes. I'll agree to anything, with one exception: she cannot be left living away from me indefinitely.” “Little Uncle!” Gu paused in surprise. “I knew you were wavering, but not that you'd change so quickly. What made you decide?” There was no reasoning out affairs between men and women. Hu had made his choice when he replaced the ‘Hu Residence’ notice. Why he had done that—whether moved by Miaozhu's sudden drawing back, or by a passing impulse—could no longer be disentangled. But he would not deceive his own conscience. Having decided, he could not betray that decision even if nobody knew of it. Taking her as his concubine today merely meant accepting his friends' goodwill and joining in the pleasure of the occasion. Yu and Gu were not the only delighted ones. Before the wedding wine was drunk, the guests were already crowding into Miaozhu's room with cheerful bridal jokes. When Miaozhen arrived, Yu and Gu acted as matchmakers and asked what terms she required. “None. It's a good thing, and I'm only happy. But I must ask Miaozhu what she wants.” Naturally, the sisters were allowed a private talk. Miaozhen feared that Hu might one day tire of her sister. He should provide money now to secure her later years, when youth and beauty had gone. “Understand me: I'm not scheming for myself. The debts from our first two years in the trade are finally cleared. I don't want a single coin. His money can be deposited or lent out in your name, and you keep the passbook. You're my sister. I'm thinking only of you.” “Then ask for three thousand taels.” Miaozhu's value should have been greater, but this marriage differed from the usual arrangement, and Miaozhen would not press her. Gu accepted the request without consulting Hu. He obtained the full amount in banknotes from Liu, who had lately been managing Hu's funds, put them in a red envelope labelled ‘Bridal Gift’, and handed it to Miaozhen. When she passed it to Miaozhu, the younger sister refused it and offered it to her elder sister in gratitude. Miaozhen would not accept. After much mutual insistence, she finally took it on the understanding that she would lend it at interest on Miaozhu's behalf.

Only when the drinking ended and the guests dispersed could Miaozhu speak with Hu. She had countless things to say, yet now did not know where to begin. Watching the tall red candles, she thought of the past two days' upheavals. Was she sad, joyful, moved or grateful? Grateful, surely, to the White-Robed Bodhisattva before whom she prayed every day. The compassionate power had answered her wish at last. Hu's feelings were much the same. In the crimson glow, everything seemed dreamlike. The lively face reflected in the mirror, equally lovely in pleasure and displeasure, filled him with excitement and pride. Then he thought of Furong in Suzhou and felt guilty. His emotions shifted so much that he too could find nothing to say. The bridal chamber was extraordinarily quiet; even the crackling candlewicks could be heard. Miaozhu became alert, then suspicious. Such a night should not be so cold and silent. She had to ask. “You regret it, don't you?” “Regret what?” he asked in surprise. “Putting up ‘Hu Residence’ yourself.” “Nothing of the sort. I never regret what I do.” She fell silent. It was some comfort, but what were his true feelings? Perhaps he denied regret while feeling it. Then she ought to regret her own rashness. The rice was cooked, but not yet swallowed. One false step must not lead to another. Better become a laughingstock than ruin her whole life. She must test his heart. The way came to her at once: to test another's sincerity, she must first show her own. Without hesitation, she opened a gilded leather trunk, took the jewel box from its bottom, unlocked it and brought it to Hu.

Inside were jade bangles, gems, rings, pearl ornaments, gold sovereigns and fragrant aloeswood beads, each wrapped in fresh cotton. As she uncovered them one by one and placed them on the table, their colours dazzled the eye. Hu did not understand. “Why are you showing off your treasures?” “These are all my private savings. Look.” She picked up a passbook and handed it to him. “Your own belongings needn't be shown to me.” Without looking, he tossed it back into the jewel box. “I estimate the jewellery at twenty thousand taels. What do you think?” “I'm no expert. Put it away quickly. Wealth shouldn't be displayed. If a thief were watching outside, there could be trouble later.” “Don't worry. The house is secure and the walls very high.” After a pause she came to the point. “I have no use for these things. Perhaps, as you say, a thief will steal them and leave me heartbroken. Better give them to you.” “What for?” “Whatever you like. They could provide some capital for your business.” Hu had many feelings at this, but finally laughed. He thought of the stories in songbooks: a young gentleman fallen on hard times, a gift of gold in a garden, triumph in the examinations, then an imperial command to return and marry his benefactress. Miaozhu seemed to harbour some such notion.

The laugh seemed slightly contemptuous. A little hurt, she said seriously, “I mean it sincerely.” “I know. Unfortunately...” He considered, then said what he had been thinking. “Your sincerity has found the wrong object.” “How can sincerity towards someone be wrong?” “The intention is good; its use is mistaken. You should have met an ambitious, poor scholar. Even if he didn't finish first in the empire, he might go to the capital and gain the jinshi degree. Then he could marry you properly as his wife and earn you an imperial title. How fine that would be.” “I don't care for that. All I want...” “What?” With difficulty, she answered, “For you not to change your heart.” Hu was silent. Of all the women he had known, Miaozhu had taken the greatest pains: first threatening death, then appealing with wealth; first fearing she could not marry him, then fearing that he would change once she had. With so many calculations, she might be hard to live with. He felt both apprehension and pity. Part of him wanted to cut the red thread they had just tied, yet he could not bear to part with her. While he hesitated, she sighed softly. “Marry a cock, follow the cock; marry a dog, follow the dog. Like you, I won't regret what I've done. The future rests with you. Whatever happens, my name is Hu now.” The words came from her heart. After that declaration, he could entertain no other plan. Yet he realized that easy promises would be unwise. He must harden himself and speak plainly first.

“With such sincerity towards me, how could I change? But I have difficulties too, and you must understand them. If circumstances force me to make you bear some hardship, will you grit your teeth and accept it?” Miaozhu clenched her teeth and gave one word: “Yes.” “Good. We needn't discuss what hardships now. Put yourself in my place when the time comes, and you'll understand that I have no choice.” The words were too vague. She had to ask. “Tell me what you mean, so I can prepare myself.” “For instance, I must leave early tomorrow and leave you alone here. Won't that be hard on you?” “That doesn't count. What else?” He shook his head. “I can't list everything now. They will be things beyond my control. Let's talk about tomorrow. Once I've left, what will you do?” “Close my doors and live quietly, of course.” He could have predicted that answer. Hearing it aloud, however, made him consider it, and a question followed. “You're used to a lively life. Can you endure the loneliness?” It was a frank, practical question, but she disliked it. Defiance entered her voice. “Wait and see whether I can.” And if she could not? Hu thought. An affair would disgrace him. This was serious; he must find a sound arrangement. The rice was already cooked. He could not pretend otherwise. There was only one course.

After all his indecision over this marriage, Hu recovered his usual clarity and firmness. “Miaozhu, put these things away for now. When there's an opportunity, I'll do some small trading for you. They are your private assets; I won't touch them for myself. As for leaving you here alone, I can't feel easy about that either. Once I go tomorrow, begin packing. I'll come back for you. I mean to settle you in Shanghai.” At last there was a definite decision. After so many twists, she had drawn out his real intention, and was deeply relieved. But there was still Furong. What would become of her? “And the one in Suzhou?” “You mean Furong?” He answered without hesitation. “I'll settle her in Huzhou.” It was plain enough to her. He meant to establish three households: the old family home in Hangzhou, and others in Shanghai and Huzhou. Shanghai was prosperous, and business would keep him there often. Her position was the best of the three. She had schemed and acted for too long to conceal her true feelings any more. Putting away her jewel box beside the pillows, she sat close against him, wrapped both arms round his upper body, laid her face against his shoulder and drew a deep breath, looking utterly content and at peace.
